issues.legal_issue: Compensation for fruit-bearing trees on surrendered surplus land is calculated using the applicable annual rate over the trees’ remaining productive years, rather than for one year only.
material_facts: The landholders surrendered surplus agricultural land containing fruit-bearing cashew trees.
A district notification set seigniorage rates for fruit-bearing trees and stated that the rates were per tree per year, with the trees yielding over their productive life.
The authorities treated the amount as payable for one year only, while the landholders claimed compensation for the full stated productive life.
issues.conclusion: The annual seigniorage rate applies across the trees’ remaining productive years, so the State’s one-year calculation was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, and clause 3 of its Second Schedule provide for payment for land and prescribe that amounts for fruit-bearing trees be calculated as prescribed; Rule 11 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Rules, 1974, links tree compensation to notified seigniorage rates. The Court read the notification according to its clear terms and held that courts cannot add to, subtract from, or alter unambiguous language to advance a perceived statutory purpose. It relied on, among others, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Price Waterhouse, Crawford v. Spooner, State of Gujarat v. Dilipbhai Nathjibhai Patel, Stock v. Frank Jones (Tipton) Ltd., Jamma Masjid, Mercara v. Kodimaniandra Deviah, Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama, Commissioner of Sales Tax, M.P. v. Popular Trading Company, Maulavi Hussein Haji Abraham Umarji v. State of Gujarat, and State of Jharkhand v. Govind Singh.

predicates.ceiling_land_compensation_appeal: A party appealed a decision determining compensation for trees on agricultural land surrendered as surplus under a land-ceiling process.
predicates.surplus_land_surrendered: The landholder surrendered agricultural land found to exceed the applicable holding limit.
predicates.fruit_bearing_trees_transferred: Fruit-bearing trees stood on the surrendered land and passed with it to the government.
predicates.schedule_sets_annual_rate: The applicable rate schedule stated a rate for each tree for each year.
predicates.schedule_states_productive_life: The rate schedule stated that the trees would yield over a specified productive life.
predicates.trees_have_remaining_productive_years: The trees had not yet completed their productive life when the land was surrendered.

issues.definition: When surplus land with fruit-bearing trees is surrendered and the applicable schedule sets annual rates over a productive life, compensation uses the annual rate for the productive years remaining at surrender.

issues.legal_issue: A landholder is not entitled to compensation for the trees’ entire productive life when part of that life had elapsed before the land was surrendered.
material_facts: The cashew trees were 12 years old when the landholders surrendered the land.
The notification specified rates by tree age and stated that the trees yielded over a 30-year life.
The landholders claimed compensation for the full 30 years, while the State maintained that compensation was due only for one year.
issues.conclusion: Compensation was payable only for the balance of the trees’ productive life after surrender, calculated using the applicable rate for trees of their age.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, clause 3 of its Second Schedule, and Rule 11 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Rules, 1974, govern the amount payable for surrendered land and fruit-bearing trees. The Court applied the notification’s age-based annual rates and productive-life terms: because the trees had already completed part of their productive life, compensation covered only the remaining years. It also applied the principle that clear text must be given effect without judicially adding or changing words, relying on authorities including Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Price Waterhouse, Crawford v. Spooner, State of Gujarat v. Dilipbhai Nathjibhai Patel, and Jamma Masjid, Mercara v. Kodimaniandra Deviah.
